summary: At supper on His last night, Jesus rises, ties a towel around Himself and washes His disciples’ feet, then tells them to follow His example.
key_insight: John begins with what Jesus knew: the Father had given all things into His hands, and He had come from God and was going to God (13:3). The towel was not taken up by someone unsure of His place. Knowing His full authority, Jesus knelt and did a servant’s work.
story: It was just before the Feast of the Passover. Jesus knew that His hour had come to depart from this world to the Father. “Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end.”

They were at supper. The devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot to betray Him. Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into His hands, and that He had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper and laid aside His garments. He tied a towel around His waist, poured water into a basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and dry them with the towel.

When He came to Simon Peter, Peter said, “Lord, are You washing my feet?” Jesus answered, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but you will know after this.” Peter said, “You shall never wash my feet!” Jesus replied, “If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me.” So Peter said, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
Jesus told him, “He who is bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is completely clean; and you are clean, but not all of you.” He knew who would betray Him.

When He had washed their feet, He put His garments back on, sat down again, and asked, “Do you know what I have done to you? You call Me Teacher and Lord, and you say well, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” He had given them an example to follow. A servant is not greater than his master. “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.”

He was not speaking of all of them. He knew whom He had chosen, but the Scripture must be fulfilled: “He who eats bread with Me has lifted up his heel against Me.” He told them before it happened, so that when it came to pass they would believe “that I am He.” Whoever received those He sent would receive Him, and whoever received Him would receive the One who sent Him.

scene.label: Washing feet
scene.text: People walked dusty roads in sandals, so a host offered water for guests to wash their feet (Genesis 18:4; Luke 7:44). The washing itself was a servant’s task, and a lowly one. When Abigail wanted to show the deepest humility, she offered to be “a servant to wash the feet of the servants” (1 Samuel 25:41).

scene.label: Garments laid aside
scene.text: Jesus took off His outer robe and tied a towel around His waist, dressed like a household servant. John uses the same words for laying aside and taking up His garments that Jesus used for laying down His life and taking it again (10:17–18).

scene.label: Bathed and washed
scene.text: A guest who had bathed at home needed only to rinse the feet that got dirty on the way. Many read Jesus’ words as using the custom to speak of two cleansings: the full washing that makes a person His, and the washing from daily sin that His own still need.

scene.label: The same evening
scene.text: Luke records that at this supper the disciples argued over which of them was the greatest, and Jesus said, “I am among you as the One who serves” (Luke 22:24–27). John does not say whether the foot washing came before or after that dispute, but the two belong together.

scene.label: Lifting the heel
scene.text: Jesus quotes Psalm 41:9, David’s grief over “my own familiar friend in whom I trusted, Who ate my bread.” Sharing bread bound people in friendship, so the betrayal of a table companion was especially bitter. Lifting the heel probably pictures a sudden kick.

witnesses.john: Only John records the foot washing. He does not retell the bread and cup, which the other Gospels had already given, but opens the second half of his Gospel with this act of love “to the end.” The scene pictures Jesus’ whole mission: He rises, lays aside His garments, stoops to serve and cleanse, then takes His garments again and sits down (compare Philippians 2:6–9).

seeing.reveals: The Lord and Teacher, holding all things in His hands, kneels with a towel before men who will desert Him and one who will betray Him. His love goes to the end, and His cleansing is not optional: “If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me.”
seeing.living: Peter first refused to be served, then wanted more than Jesus offered. Let Jesus wash you on His terms, then take up the towel yourself. He washed the feet of Judas too, so following His example means serving the people who will not thank you, not only the ones who honor you.
seeing.ponder: Is it harder for you to let Jesus serve you, or to kneel before the person you least want to serve?

preaching.big_idea: Knowing all authority was His, Jesus took a towel; His followers must do the same.
outline: Love that goes to the end (1–3)
preaching.watch_for: Verse 3 begins with what Jesus knew; verse 17 ends with what the disciples now know: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” Knowing who Jesus is leads straight to a towel.
